CRISPR slash Cas nine. It's a genome-editing tool adapted from bacterial immune systems that uses a guide RNA to direct the Cas nine nuclease to cut DNA at precise locations, enabling deletion, correction, or insertion of genetic sequences. Its programmability, simplicity, and efficiency have revolutionized genetic engineering and hold promise for treating genetic diseases. CRISPR-Cas is a natural defense mechanism in bacteria and archaea against viral infection. The system stores fragments of invader DNA in repeating sequences. A synthetic RNA between twenty and thirty nucleotides directs Cas nine to the target DNA sequence. By changing the guide sequence, you reprogram the system to edit different genes without redesigning the nuclease itself. The nuclease cuts both strands of DNA at the target site, and then the cell's repair machinery either disables the gene through non-homologous end joining, or NHEJ, or incorporates a new sequence if a template is provided through a process called homology-directed repair, or HDR. The guide RNA can partially match unintended sites, causing unwanted edits—called off-target effects—though careful guide design and delivery minimizes this risk. Multiple guides can direct Cas nine to edit several sites simultaneously, enabling complex edits through multiplexing. Applications include correcting cystic fibrosis mutations, engineering disease-resistant crops, and developing cancer immunotherapies. This technique connects to DNA as the genome substrate being edited, Cas nine as the nuclease enzyme from Streptococcus pyogenes, genome editing as the broader field of targeted genetic modification, molecular cloning as CRISPR integrates new sequences with cloning techniques delivering the CRISPR machinery, and gene therapy as the therapeutic application of CRISPR-edited cells.
